content: Rotavirus is primarily transmitted through close person-to-person contact or indirectly via contaminated objects and surfaces, such as toys or environmental surfaces that have been exposed to stool. Transmission through contaminated water or food is considered uncommon. The virus is highly contagious, with an infectious dose as low as fewer than 100 viral particles. The incubation period for rotavirus is short, typically less than 48 hours, with a range of 24 to 72 hours. The illness usually lasts between 3 to 7 days, but in some cases, it may persist for 2 to 3 weeks. The period of communicability begins two days before the onset of diarrhea and continues for several days after symptoms appear. This includes the acute phase of the disease and the period during which viral shedding persists. Estimating the case fatality ratio for rotavirus is challenging, as it largely depends on access to healthcare services, particularly for rehydration therapy. Currently available rotavirus vaccines are live, oral, attenuated strains derived from human and/or animal origins. These vaccines replicate in the human intestine to stimulate an immune response. The World Health Organization (WHO) has prequalified four vaccines: Rotarix, RotaTeq, Rotavac, and Rotasiil. All of these vaccines have demonstrated good safety profiles. While there is an association between rotavirus vaccines and intussusception, no other serious adverse events have been identified. One of the earliest rotavirus vaccines, RotaShield, was linked to intussusception. However, a recent Cochrane review of the four WHO-prequalified vaccines found no increased risk of intussusception in randomized controlled trials for any of the vaccines. In 2016, rotavirus infection was estimated to cause approximately 128,500 deaths globally among children under five years of age, with a 95% uncertainty interval of 104,500 to 155,600 deaths. In the WHO South-East Asia Region, rotavirus accounted for an estimated 3,765 deaths (95% uncertainty interval: 2,895–4,789). The WHO launched the Global Rotavirus Surveillance Network in 2008 to generate local data for decision-making on vaccine introduction and sustained use, monitor disease trends and genotype distribution, and provide a platform for vaccine effectiveness studies. This network also emphasizes the importance of surveillance data for advocacy and fundraising. Surveillance officers at sentinel sites are responsible for daily monitoring of wards, maintaining a diarrhea log, enrolling eligible patients, ensuring proper specimen collection and laboratory testing, and tracking cases for timely results. They must also share findings with relevant stakeholders and maintain a regularly updated data logbook. Data management responsibilities include cleaning and validating data, maintaining a backup of the surveillance database, and analyzing core epidemiological variables. Surveillance officers must periodically review data quality to identify issues in patient enrollment, specimen collection, or testing procedures. Monitoring activities include ensuring adequate case enrollment, verifying the quality and volume of stool specimens, and addressing any challenges with laboratory testing methods. If fewer than 15% of enrolled children test positive for rotavirus, or if the youngest age groups are underrepresented, the surveillance system may require adjustments. Vaccination data should be collected from reliable sources, such as vaccination cards or medical records, and the type and number of vaccine doses administered should be documented. Stool specimens should be tested using appropriate methodologies, such as enzyme immunoassay (EIA), rapid tests, or RT-PCR, and results should be reported promptly. The WHO has developed guidelines and standards for rotavirus surveillance and laboratory capacity building to support global efforts in monitoring and controlling the disease. These efforts are guided by strategic input from regional and global experts, including WHO staff, UNICEF, and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
